keyVerseText: And if ye walk contrary unto me, and will not hearken unto me; I will bring seven times more plagues upon you according to your sins. contrary: or, at all adventures with me
rootMeaning: The Hebrew noun מַכָּה (makkâh) stems from the root נָכָה (nâkâh), which fundamentally means to strike or beat. This root conveys the action of delivering a blow, whether light or severe, and carries connotations of wounding, smiting, or causing defeat. The etymology highlights that מַכָּה is not merely a physical strike but encompasses the effect of that strike, such as a wound or plague, deepening our understanding beyond the simple English word 'blow' to include the resulting impact or judgment implied in the term.
usageInScripture: Across its 47 occurrences, מַכָּה is translated variously as 'slaughter,' 'plague,' 'wounds,' and 'stripes,' reflecting a broad semantic range from physical blows to devastating judgments. The predominance of 'slaughter' (13 times) and references to plagues indicate that the word often describes severe consequences, whether in warfare or divine punishment. This range reveals that מַכָּה conveys not only physical harm but also figurative defeat and affliction, illustrating God's righteous discipline or human suffering in biblical narrative.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding מַכָּה as a term that encompasses both physical blows and divine judgments enriches our grasp of God's holiness and justice. It reminds believers that sin brings consequences that are serious and often painful, reflecting God's righteous response to disobedience. Yet, within this, there is also the hope of restoration, as the blows or plagues are corrective rather than merely punitive. The word underscores the reality of spiritual warfare and the cost of sin, pointing ultimately to Christ who bore the ultimate 'makkâh' on our behalf, absorbing the blows of judgment so that we might be healed.
keyVerseReflection: Leviticus 26:21 warns that if the people continue to rebel, God will bring 'seven times more plagues' upon them according to their sins. Here, מַכָּה as 'plagues' emphasizes the seriousness of divine discipline as a consequence of persistent disobedience. The word conveys not just random suffering but a measured, purposeful chastisement designed to bring the people back to covenant faithfulness. This verse highlights God's justice and mercy intertwined—plagues are a severe warning but also an invitation to repentance.
